metric_rationale: This is the within-subject decline in adherence to the highest-validity cue from q=1 conflicts to strong q>=4 conflicts. TTB predicts the same top-cue adherence probability at every q for any beta and epsilon, so its expected contrast is exactly zero while subject-level nuisance parameters cancel. Tallying predicts 50% top-cue adherence at q=1 because the cue counts tie, but substantially less than 50% at q>=4 because the lower-cue majority has a margin of at least three. Pooling q=4,5,6 retains sensitivity even at low beta while averaging 48 trials per subject in the high-conflict term; mirrored stimuli remove A/B orientation from the coding.

This validity-ranked choice index is +1 when a response follows the highest-validity discriminating cue and -1 otherwise. Because every designed pair has a 3–3 tally tie, Tallying predicts an expected index of exactly 0: its random choice is unrelated to which option the ranked cue favors. Take The Best predicts a positive index of (1-epsilon)*tanh(beta/2), potentially approaching 1. The statistic uses all 96 trials per subject, including both orientations of the mirrored pairs, so random response variation averages out and between-subject variance should remain comparatively small. On human data, an index near zero specifically supports the advocated Tallying account, whereas a reliably positive value supports validity-prioritized choice.

This soft cue-8 dominance index targets the design's strongest directional dissociation. TTB chooses the feature-8 winner with probability above .50 for every allowed parameter combination, whereas accessibility-gated search is expected to choose it on only about 20–30% of trials because three accessible cues favor the opposite option. Centering the smooth transform at .40 places the transition between these prediction regions. The steep bounded transform compresses within-theory variation while retaining a large between-theory gap: TTB should yield values near 1 and the competing theory values near 0. It avoids a brittle hard classifier, uses all 96 trials, and A/B mirroring ensures that the score cannot be driven by a product-key response bias.

This is a within-subject rank-separation contrast. It measures how much more often the option favored by the higher-validity cue is selected in four- and seven-rank conflicts than in adjacent-rank conflicts. Take The Best assigns the same higher-cue choice probability to every trial regardless of rank distance, so beta, lapse rate, and general determinism cancel from the expected contrast, yielding approximately zero. Accessibility-Gated Stochastic Lexicographic Search predicts substantial lower-cue capture for adjacent conflicts but near-deterministic higher-cue choices at larger separations, yielding a positive value. Pooling the two saturated large-distance conditions reduces binomial variance, while omitting the intermediate distance-2 condition avoids diluting the contrast. A/B mirrors ensure the score is not driven by option-side preference.

The metric is a soft prevalence score for a theoretically diagnostic behavioral pattern: reliably selecting the later, much more valid cue in each adjacent-cue conflict. The advocated fixed hierarchy predicts later-cue choice rates around 0.78–0.86, whereas the gated stochastic theory predicts rates near 0.5 because validity is suppressed by its mapping gate. Centering the smooth threshold at 0.65 places it well between those regimes. Averaging all 96 mirrored observations before applying the sigmoid reduces trial noise, while the bounded transformation compresses within-theory subject variation and preserves a large between-theory difference. Computing the transformation separately by subject and then averaging also makes the pooled value an interpretable soft proportion of subjects exhibiting the diagnostic preference.

This metric measures endorsement of the option jointly supported by the first two, highly valid cues, while coding A/B mirror trials identically. The stochastic-search theory predicts that the five opposing cues collectively outweigh those two cues plus the rotating third supporter, placing the underlying endorsement rate below 0.5. Fixed lexicographic search predicts endorsement above about 0.8 because one of the first two cues normally controls choice. A prespecified smooth threshold at 0.64 lies in the wide region where neither theory predicts observations. The logistic transformation maps the two predicted regimes close to 0 and 1 while remaining continuous and substantially reducing within-regime between-subject variance. It uses all 96 trials and works unchanged for pooled data or a single-subject slice.

This is a within-subject conflict-density discontinuity score. It measures how much more often the option supported by the earliest discriminating cue is selected on sparse k=7 displays than on their dense k=9 counterparts. The advocated theory predicts a large positive value: serial control at k=7 favors the earliest cue, whereas parallel tally integration at k=9 favors its tally-majority opponent. The competing stochastic lexicographic theory uses essentially the same stable accessibility process at both densities, so it predicts similar earliest-cue choice rates and a score near zero. Using all 48 observations at each density and taking a within-subject difference limits binomial noise and cancels stable response, lapse, and accessibility tendencies.

This is the position-led stopping rate: the fraction of trials on which the subject chooses the option supported by the earliest discriminating feature. In every designed pair, the earliest cue supports the designated two-cue option, while three other cues support its opponent. Accessibility-gated stochastic search distributes first attention across all five discriminating cues and should therefore produce a rate near 0.4–0.5. The competing serial-control theory assigns substantial probability to stopping at the leading cue and predicts a markedly higher rate, approximately 0.6–0.7. Pooling all 96 trials gives a low-noise subject-level estimate, while the mirrored A/B trials make the measure insensitive to a general response-side bias.
